title: One in Three World Cup Matches Faces Dangerous Heat. FIFA Just Banned Fans From Bringing Water Bottles.
excerpt: With the tournament kicking off on June 11 across 16 North American cities, an NPR analysis finds 39 matches at high risk for heat illness — and diaspora fans attending in Houston, Dallas, and Miami face the worst conditions.
body:
The largest FIFA World Cup in history begins next week across the United States, Canada, and Mexico, and the biggest threat to players and fans may not come from the opposing team. It may come from the weather.

An NPR analysis of two decades of temperature data across all 16 host cities found that more than one-third of the tournament's 104 matches — 39 in total — face high risk for dangerously hot and humid conditions. Another 28 carry moderate risk. The metric used, wet bulb globe temperature, accounts for humidity, shade, and solar radiation, making it a more reliable indicator of heat danger than air temperature alone.

## The Stadiums Where Risk Is Highest

Miami, Houston, Dallas, and Atlanta rank as the hottest venue cities, with historical averages reaching 84°F during match times. While those stadiums have air conditioning, cities such as Philadelphia, New Jersey, and Kansas City have open-air venues with no roofs — and average temperatures as high as 79°F.

The World Cup final itself, scheduled for 3 p.m. on July 19 at MetLife Stadium outside New York City, sits in one of the highest-risk slots. "If you schedule these matches for the midafternoon at some of these hottest locations, then that's your recipe for disaster," warned Donal Mullan, a climate scientist at Queen's University Belfast who co-authored a peer-reviewed study on heat risk at the 2026 tournament.

## FIFA's Bottle Ban Drew Immediate Backlash

Against this backdrop, FIFA updated its stadium code of conduct this week to prohibit spectators from bringing reusable water bottles into venues — reversing an earlier assurance that fans could carry their own. Inside stadiums, water bottles will cost $4 to $7.50, while beer will be available for as little as $8.19.

Medical professionals called the decision "alarming." The UK Health Security Agency's own guidelines state that heatstroke is a medical emergency and that regular fluid intake is essential to prevent dehydration. Combining alcohol consumption with high temperatures and humidity creates what researchers call a "synergistic effect" — elevated core temperature, reduced sweat production, and accelerated dehydration.

## The Precedents Are Alarming

This is not hypothetical. During a June 2024 international match in Kansas City, referee Humberto Panjoj collapsed on the field from heat illness and was hospitalised. At a separate 2024 match in Miami, a star Uruguay player left at halftime suffering dizziness and dehydration. In 2017, professional footballer Rachel Daly collapsed from heat exhaustion during a match in Houston despite additional water breaks.

In 2023, a university student died waiting for a Taylor Swift concert in Brazil during a heatwave. In 2024, over 1,300 pilgrims died during the Hajj when extreme heat struck Saudi Arabia. Large gatherings amplify heat risk because attendees are in unfamiliar environments with limited knowledge of where to find water, shade, or medical care.

## What This Means for Diaspora Fans

India is playing in the World Cup for the first time in modern history, and tens of thousands of NRI fans are expected to attend matches. Many will be travelling to cities like Houston, Dallas, and Miami — the three highest-risk venues — from cooler home bases in the Bay Area, Pacific Northwest, or the Northeast.

The combination of jet lag, unfamiliar climates, alcohol availability, and the emotional intensity of supporting India in its first World Cup creates a compounding risk that most diaspora fans have never experienced at a sporting event. The practical advice is unglamorous but potentially lifesaving: hydrate aggressively the day before and the morning of the match, avoid alcohol until after the final whistle, wear light-coloured clothing, and know where the nearest medical tent is before you need it.

FIFA says it will "activate additional cooling capacity, including shaded areas, misting systems, cooling buses and expanded water distribution" when temperatures warrant. It did not specify what temperature threshold would trigger those protections, nor whether stadium workers would have the same access as spectators.

## The Bigger Picture

Climate change is making these decisions harder. The last decade was the hottest on record. North American heat waves are growing longer and more intense. The Qatar World Cup was moved to winter entirely because of heat concerns. The 2026 tournament was not.

For NRI families planning trips around India's group-stage matches, the calculus now includes a variable that no one put on the packing list: heat risk. Check the kick-off time, check the venue, and plan accordingly. The match you flew across the country to attend should not become a medical emergency.

*Sources: NPR analysis of WBGT data across 16 host cities (June 2026); The Sun (FIFA bottle ban, June 2026); Queen's University Belfast study on 2026 World Cup heat risk; World Weather Attribution / Imperial College London (May 2026); Audacy / NIH (alcohol and heat research)*
